I will admit that encryption is still being studied and a lot of concepts haven't been discovered yet, but the odds of someone like me getting 'hacked' has dropped to pretty much zero when I took a few minutes of my day (not including waiting for it to encrypt) to protect myself.

The only way for someone to gain access to my files is either:

  • gaining access to my computer while my computer is decrypted while in use
  • knowing my 32-character password to decrypt it
  • using a cold boot attack to retrieve encryption keys, which requires physical access to my running (as in 'on') machine
  • finding a security hole in my encryption hardware [Edit: software; I don't have encryption hardware]

I have it setup so all of the above have been minimized. I never leave my computer on or decrypted when not logged in, and I have a special script run by a memorized key combination to gracefully re-encrypt and shut down my computer in case of an emergency (unlikely, but I accounted for it).

It is possible to keep a computer secure; you just need to learn how to do it. Not everyone has the time or patience to lock down their machines as much as I did, but even encrypting a hard drive or flash drive with personal files doesn't require a computer genius. You just need to know three things:

  • encrypt your private, personal files with government-grade encryption and a strong, impossible-to-guess password
  • keep these private files inside the encryption container as much as possible: do not copy the files to an unencrypted system or drive; try to prevent unwanted eyes on your encryption container (people over the Internet, friends overlooking your shoulder, hackers); etc.
  • act like your encrypted container doesn't even exist: hackers can't really hack something they don't even exists

Well, I don't have any quick references to read up on, since most of the knowledge I've acquired was over the years finding ways to encrypt my personal files. A general understanding of encryption can be found on the Wikipedia article about it (and external links). I do want to leave you with some knowledge, though, so I'm going to explain the process I use to keep my files secure.

The Tools

I only really need two things to keep my files secure:

  • My computer

  • Encryption software: I use a software called TrueCrypt. TrueCrypt is cross-platform encryption software that's really easy to use and can be customized to many different situations, from simple non-tech people to people like me who take security and privacy seriously.

    If you want to try TrueCrypt out yourself, I recommend downloading it, but not from the website, since it seems fishy lately. It has been discontinued, but the source is available.

    I recommend downloading it from https://truecrypt.ch/, which is the unofficial download for a more stable version (I got my TrueCrypt downloads from there and they're clean of any sort of malware). The version that'll download is actually an official version, 7.1a, a version released before the website became weird and the project was discontinued.

    Don't worry, though. There is no known security issues with the software, so I still consider it a great encryption tool.

The Process

This whole process is mainly a first-time setup that takes some time, but, afterwards, it only requires a password (and a keyfile if you choose) to access and forget about the encryption to use the computer normally. This is my exact setup, so I'm not expecting you to go full out like I am (not even sure if you even find this information valuable), but I hope you take something from it — feel free to ask me further about it if you need.

Step 1: Drive Partitions

The first thing I do is partition my hard drive into two partitions:

  • an unencrypted partition for global applications (source code editors, video editors, video games, etc.) and the operating system
  • a soon-to-be-encrypted partition for personal files and identity-sensitive applications (web browsers, tax software, etc.)

Typically, one-third of my hard drive will be partitioned for global applications/OS and the other two-thirds for the encrypted partition. I do this because I do a lot of video editing and various other heavy-file organizing. The amount can be adjusted to anything, really (as long as you give the OS enough breathing room, of course).

Step 2: TrueCrypt Encryption

After the disk partitions are ready, I launch TrueCrypt to encrypt the soon-to-be-encrypted partition so we can keep our files secure. I set a long, secure password (kind of looks like this: 8uYrqr(/v4xwXt) and wait for it to encrypt. For bigger partitions, like 300+ GB, it will take a few hours. The optimal time to do this is right before going to bed or work or to a party or something.

Step 3: Installing Programs

Now it's time to install the programs. I mentally sort through all of the programs, one by one, on whether or not they'll have any personal information in them. I use portable versions of these programs on my encrypted partition because I sync it with my laptop so I can have identical work environments. If this doesn't appeal to you, you can just regularly install the program as normal, just inside the encrypted partition.

Step 4: Setting Up Startup

This is an important step. If you're doing it like I am, you will run into issues because sometimes the operating system will freak out on startup if it can't find any file or folder that actually belongs to the encrypted partition. An example of this (which frustrated me because I kept forgetting about it) is Microsoft OneDrive making itself startup automatically before it gives me a chance to unlock my encrypted partition, then freaking out because it can't find the folder.

Disable any program from starting up automatically before you're able to unlock your encrypted partition or drive. To be safe, I disable anything except TrueCrypt from automatically starting up. Well, what if I don't want to relaunch all of my programs every single time I unlock it? That's where a custom startup script comes in handy.

At this point it's strictly Windows (everything else is generally cross-platform), but I'm sure there's ways to duplicate this method on other platforms. I create a folder in my encrypted partition called Startup. I put it in the Application folder I have, along with all my other portable apps. Then, we create a batch script and place it in the root directory:

@echo off
taskkill /f /IM explorer.exe
start explorer.exe
for %%v in ("L:\Application\Startup\*.lnk") do start "" "%%~v"

This basically ends the explorer.exe process (in case it has a handle on anything in the encrypted partition; just a safety precaution), then restarts it (basically 'refreshing' it). Then, it executes all shortcut files (that point to programs in the Startup folder you want to automatically launch at this point) in that Startup folder we set up.

I have it down to a routine at this point:

  1. TrueCrypt is launched and I enter my password to unlock my encrypted partition. TrueCrypt automatically opens the folder pointing to the partition location after it's unlocked.
  2. Since the Startup.bat file is in this folder that it opened up, all I have to do is double-click on the batch file and it acts like a pseudo-startup, closing that file window and launching the programs I want.
  3. Start using the computer like normal.

In Conclusion

Yeah, it's a lot of details and I don't expect you to go as far as I do in encrypting personal files. I have a lot of other methods I use to keep my privacy safe and emergency script files to protect my encryption, but that's a conversation for another day.

I'm not an expert at encryption, but I know how to use it to my advantage. There are many things to learn about it, including PC encrypting (which this little guide was), cloud encryption (for things like Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, etc.), and others. Feel free to ask anything you'd like about either encryption itself or the processes.

That's about all I can say for tonight, since it's already past my bedtime. Please forgive my lack of proof-reading — I'll fix anything tomorrow. Take care! :-)
